newsitem.title: THAILAND: At least 60 Burmese opposition leaders held - NLD.
newsitem.headline: At least 60 Burmese opposition leaders held - NLD.

text.p: At least 60 senior members of Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) have been arrested by Burma's military government, and the number is expected to grow, a top NLD official said on Thursday.

The official told Reuters by telephone from Rangoon that the NLD members were mostly from the provinces and had been detained as they headed to the capital to attend a party meeting scheduled for May 27.
"It is more than 60 now, I believe," the NLD official said, speaking from Suu Kyi's house. Most of those arrested were members of parliament (MPs) elected in a 1990 poll.

The NLD won more than 80 percent of the seats in the May 27, 1990 election. But the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) never recognised the result and has cracked down on elected MPs and top party organisers ever since.
The NLD official said he was sure the number of people detained would rise over the next few days as news trickled in from the provinces.
Government officials were not immediately available for comment on the arrests.
The party official said the NLD would still hold its May 27 anniversary celebration, which would double as a party meeting.
"We are a political party, and we have to do our job," he said. "People will be coming. They will get here in their own way."

The official said several MPs who had reached Rangoon were staying in Suu Kyi's compound, where the meeting was to be held. He said the Nobel Peace laureate, who had been rumoured to be ill, was fine but was busy and could not come to the telephone.

There were reports that NLD MPs and top party organisers were detained in their homes, followed in buses as they headed to Rangoon, or warned not to attend the meeting on threat of arrest, the official added.
More than 261 top NLD members, most of them elected MPs, were arrested in connection with a party congress last May that was timed to coincide with the anniversary of the 1990 poll.
The SLORC said then that they had only detained them temporarily for questioning in order to prevent anarchy.

Many were later released, although Suu Kyi said authorities had forced many of the MPs to sign papers promising to resign from the party. Some of those not released were charged and sentenced to long prison terms.
News of the arrests drew condemnation from the United States and human rights organisations.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday that the arrests demonstrated the "perfidious and inhumane nature" of the SLORC regime.
"It's another reason why we don't think Burma should be treated as a normal country," Burns said one day after President Bill Clinton officially imposed economic sanctions on Burma.
Amnesty International condemned the arrests and called for their immediate and unconditional release.
The London-based human rights organization said more than 2,000 people in Burma were arrested in 1996, the majority of them NLD members or supporters.
